lines: Title: all poly's such that $P(n)$ divides $2^n-1$
Find all polynomials $P$ with integer coefficients such that $P(n)$ divides $2^n-1$ for all positive integers $n$.
Context (from a comment by the OP): it's my own problem formulated while I was reading articles on Mersenne primes, I don't have any results (neither mine nor founded)
Here’s another proof, which I believe is simpler. Let $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be such a polynomial. Then, note that $P(n)|P(2n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Let $f, g \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be s.t. $g(n)|f(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then, $f = rg$ for some $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
By considering the limiting behaviour of the ratio as $n \to \infty$, clearly we must have that $k = l$. We also deduce that $\frac{a_k}{b_k} = r \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let $D$ denote the difference operator which acts as $(Df)(n) = f(n+1) - f(n)$. Note that if $f(n) = rg(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(D^j f)(n) = r(D^jg)(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. We conclude the proof by induction on $j$ with the claim that $D^j f = r D^j g \implies D^{(j-1)} f = r D^{(j-1)}g$.

For the basis, let $j = k$ and note that $(D^kf)(n) = r(D^kg)(n)$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ -- with both $D^kf$ and $D^kg$ polynomials of degree $0$ i.e. constants -- so we trivially have that $D^k f = r D^k g$. The induction step then follows by "integrating" the differences. At each step, there is a constant of integration, but the condition $(D^j f)(n) = r(D^jg)(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ along with the inductive hypothesis forces the constants for $f,g$ to have ratio $r$ as desired. $\square$
Returning to the broader proof, we deduce that $P(2n) = rP(n)$ for some $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Suppose $r \neq \pm 1$. Then, $P$ must have degree at most $1$ with constant term $0$. If $P(n) \equiv an$, then we must have $a|2^n-1$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, so $a = \pm 1$. This reduces the problem to proving that $n \not | 2^n-1$ (for the question, technically even one counterexample suffices). The general statement can be proved as in the link in the other answer.
Otherwise, $r = \pm 1$. In this case, $P$ takes the same value infinitely often, so it must be constant, and we easily conclude that $P \equiv 1$ or $P \equiv -1$. $\square$
